2	name: blueprint-conventions
3	description: The LaTeX-subset blueprint format and house style — environments, \uses/\lean/\leanok/\mathlibok/\notready, the math-purity rule, and complete (not sketched) proofs.
4	---
5	
6	Blueprints are a LaTeX subset (the `leanblueprint` dialect) parsed into the DAG.
7	Write timeless mathematics — a standalone document, not a project journal.
8	
9	## Environments
10	
11	Each declaration is an amsthm-style environment; the recognized ones are
12	`theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`,
13	`example`, `notation`, `convention`, and `proof`. A statement environment plus
14	its following `proof` environment form one node's content.
15	
16	## Per-node macros
17	
18	- `\label{id}` — a stable id (the DAG node key).
19	- `\lean{Name}` — the Lean declaration(s) this node formalizes; comma-separate to
20	  bind several (`\lean{a, b}`) when they jointly formalize the node's statement.
21	  Each named declaration's signature must match the statement. The mapping need
22	  not be 1-to-1: a node may name several declarations, and Lean may carry
23	  auxiliary declarations with no node at all.
24	- `\uses{a,b}` — dependencies on other nodes' labels; these drive the DAG edges.
25	  Add an edge instead of re-explaining a dependency in prose. Put `\uses` in the
26	  statement for definitional deps and in the `proof` for deps used only in the
27	  proof.
28	- `\source{slug:page-0001}` — reference anchors for UI popups and audit trails.
29	  Use page-level ids from `references/<slug>/tex/page-0001.tex` or an equivalent
30	  manifest entry. Multiple anchors may be comma-separated.
31	- `\leanok` — the Lean is written and checked. Honest only when its Lean is
32	  actually checked *and* its dependencies are too. On a `proof`, it means the
33	  proof is formalized; on a statement, the signature is formalized.
34	- `\mathlibok` — the declaration is already available in mathlib (no
35	  formalization needed; treat as a leaf).
36	
37	## House style
38	
39	- **Pure mathematics only.** No Lean tactics, typeclass/implementation notes, or
40	  semi-Lean pseudocode. No project history ("since iter N", "our failed route")
41	  and no conversational filler. Not every Lean helper needs its own node —
42	  auxiliary or implementation-only declarations can stay unnoded; add a node when
43	  the result is mathematically meaningful in its own right. In particular, never
44	  add a `Formalization note` paragraph to blueprint `.tex`: attach implementation
45	  details, failed approaches, and mechanization caveats to the statement's hgraph
46	  node with `horizon graph ... add comment` instead.
47	- **Complete proofs, not sketches.** A node's `proof` is a real, rigorous
48	  mathematical proof a reader could check — not a hand-wave or a TODO. The way to
49	  keep it short is to *split*, not to abbreviate: if a proof is long or a node
50	  grows past a short paragraph, break out the hard step as its own `\uses`-linked
51	  lemma (down to sentence-sized lemmas if needed) so each node stays small and
52	  its proof stays complete.
53	- **One statement's worth per node.** Keep each node to a single mathematical
54	  statement; don't restate Lean source as prose.
55	- **Cite by source link, not quote comments.** Add `\source{...}` to the
56	  relevant node. Keep the retrieved/transcribed page text in `references/` (for
57	  example `references/<slug>/tex/page-0042.tex`) and let the UI expose it; do not
58	  paste verbatim source quotes into `% QUOTE` comments inside the blueprint.

1	\chapter{The Jacobian as an abelian variety}
2	\label{chap:Jacobian}
3	
4	Let \(C\) be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over a field
5	\(k\), with genus \(g(C)\).  The Jacobian is constructed uniformly as the
6	identity component \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) of the Picard scheme.  It is an abelian
7	variety of dimension \(g(C)\); when \(g(C)=0\), it is \(\Spec k\).
8	
9	\section{Albanese objects}
10	
11	\begin{definition}[Albanese universal property of a pointed curve]\leanok
12	  \label{def:IsAlbanese}
13	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.IsAlbanese}
14	  Let \(P \in C(k)\).  An abelian variety \(J\) together with a pointed
15	  morphism \(\iota_P \colon C \to J\) is an \emph{Albanese object} for
16	  \((C,P)\) if every pointed morphism \(f \colon C \to A\) to an abelian
17	  variety factors uniquely through \(\iota_P\): there is a unique morphism of
18	  \(k\)-schemes \(g \colon J \to A\) such that
19	  \[
20	    P \circ \iota_P = \eta_J,
21	    \qquad
22	    f = \iota_P \circ g.
23	  \]
24	\end{definition}
25	
26	\begin{remark}
27	  \label{rem:IsAlbanese_typeclasses}
28	  The phrase ``abelian variety'' includes the group structure, properness,
29	  smoothness, and geometric irreducibility of both \(J\) and every target
30	  \(A\).  These are hypotheses of the universal property, rather than extra
31	  conclusions inside it.
32	\end{remark}
33	
34	\subsection{The universal morphism}
35	
36	\begin{definition}[The Albanese universal morphism]\leanok
37	  \label{def:IsAlbanese_ofCurve}
38	  \uses{def:IsAlbanese}
39	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.IsAlbanese.ofCurve}
40	  An Albanese structure on \((C,P,J)\) determines a distinguished morphism
41	  \(\iota_P \colon C \to J\), called its universal morphism.
42	\end{definition}
43	
44	\begin{lemma}[Pointed condition]\leanok
45	  \label{lem:IsAlbanese_comp_ofCurve}
46	  \uses{def:IsAlbanese, def:IsAlbanese_ofCurve}
47	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.IsAlbanese.comp_ofCurve}
48	  The universal morphism satisfies \(P \circ \iota_P = \eta_J\).
49	\end{lemma}
50	
51	\begin{lemma}[Universal factorisation]\leanok
52	  \label{lem:IsAlbanese_exists_unique_ofCurve_comp}
53	  \uses{def:IsAlbanese, def:IsAlbanese_ofCurve}
54	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.IsAlbanese.exists_unique_ofCurve_comp}
55	  Every pointed morphism \(f \colon C \to A\) to an abelian variety factors
56	  uniquely as \(f=\iota_P\circ g\) through a morphism of \(k\)-schemes
57	  \(g \colon J \to A\).
58	\end{lemma}
59	
60	\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of the Albanese object]\leanok
61	  \label{thm:IsAlbanese_unique}
62	  \uses{def:IsAlbanese, def:IsAlbanese_ofCurve}
63	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.IsAlbanese.unique}
64	  If \((J_1,\iota_1)\) and \((J_2,\iota_2)\) are Albanese objects for
65	  \((C,P)\), there is a unique morphism \(e \colon J_1\to J_2\) satisfying
66	  \(\iota_2=\iota_1\circ e\).
67	\end{theorem}
68	
69	\begin{proof}\leanok
70	  The universal property of \(J_1\) applied to \(\iota_2\) gives
71	  \(e \colon J_1\to J_2\); that of \(J_2\) applied to \(\iota_1\) gives
72	  \(e' \colon J_2\to J_1\).  Both \(e\circ e'\) and the identity of \(J_1\)
73	  factor \(\iota_1\) through itself, so uniqueness gives
74	  \(e\circ e'=\mathrm{id}_{J_1}\); similarly
75	  \(e'\circ e=\mathrm{id}_{J_2}\).  The original universal property gives the
76	  required uniqueness of \(e\).
77	\end{proof}
78	
79	\begin{remark}
80	  \label{rem:IsAlbanese_unique_iso}
81	  Consequently the Albanese object is unique up to a unique isomorphism
82	  compatible with the universal morphism.
83	\end{remark}
84	
85	\section{A uniform Jacobian witness}
86	
87	\begin{definition}[Jacobian witness]\leanok
88	  \label{def:JacobianWitness}
89	  \uses{def:IsAlbanese, def:genus}
90	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianWitness}
91	  A \emph{Jacobian witness} for \(C\) consists of a single \(k\)-scheme \(J\),
92	  an abelian-variety structure on \(J\), a proof that \(J\) is smooth of
93	  relative dimension \(g(C)\), and, for every \(P\in C(k)\), an Albanese
94	  structure on \((C,P,J)\).
95	\end{definition}
96	
97	\begin{remark}
98	  \label{rem:JacobianWitness_quantifier_order}
99	  The same \(J\) works for every marked point.  Replacing \(P\) by another
100	  rational point translates the universal morphism by an automorphism of
101	  \(J\), so it does not change the underlying abelian variety.
102	\end{remark}
103	
104	\begin{remark}
105	  \label{rem:JacobianWitness_smooth_redundancy}
106	  Smoothness is implied by smoothness of relative dimension \(g(C)\).  It is
107	  nevertheless useful to record both the abelian-variety property and the
108	  dimension assertion as parts of the witness.
109	\end{remark}
110	
111	\subsection{The Picard witness \(J=\Pic^0_{C/k}\)}
112	\label{sec:picardJacobianWitness}
113	
114	\begin{theorem}[A Jacobian witness for a pointed curve]
115	  \label{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint}
116	  \uses{def:JacobianWitness, def:genus, thm:fga_pic_representability,
117	    thm:pic0_isAbelianVariety, thm:pic_zero_dimension_equals_genus,
118	    thm:albanese_universal_property_northstar, def:has_rational_point}
119	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint}
120	  Let \(C\) be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over \(k\)
121	  possessing a \(k\)-rational point. Then the identity component
122	  \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) carries a Jacobian witness for \(C\).
123	\end{theorem}
124	
125	\begin{proof}
126	  \uses{lem:curve_geometrically_integral, def:inst_has_pic_scheme,
127	    lem:pic0_relative_dimension_genus, lem:pic0_isAlbanese_all_points}
128	  Representability of the relative Picard functor
129	  (\cref{def:inst_has_pic_scheme}, whose hypothesis is the rational point) gives
130	  \(\Pic_{C/k}\), and its identity component \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) is a group scheme,
131	  smooth, proper and geometrically irreducible by
132	  \cref{thm:pic0_isAbelianVariety}. Those four data are the first four fields of
133	  the witness; of the four, \cref{thm:pic0_smooth} and \cref{thm:pic0_proper} are
134	  the ones whose own proofs are still open.
135	
136	  Three further steps are needed, and each is isolated as a lemma because it does
137	  not follow from the four above.
138	
139	  First, the hypotheses must be reconciled: \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) is constructed for a
140	  geometrically \emph{integral} curve, whereas a witness is required for a
141	  geometrically irreducible one. Geometric integrality is automatic
142	  (\cref{lem:curve_geometrically_integral}).
143	
144	  Second, the smoothness supplied by \cref{thm:pic0_isAbelianVariety} carries no
145	  relative dimension, while the witness records smoothness at the specific
146	  relative dimension \(g(C)\); the tangent-space identification
147	  \(T_0\Pic^0_{C/k}\cong H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\) of
148	  \cref{thm:pic_zero_dimension_equals_genus} supplies the dimension, and
149	  \cref{lem:pic0_relative_dimension_genus} is the resulting refinement.
150	
151	  Third, the Albanese structure is required for \emph{every} \(P\in C(k)\) and for
152	  every genus, whereas \cref{thm:albanese_universal_property_northstar} is proved
153	  over an algebraically closed base field and for \(g(C) > 0\); the extension is
154	  \cref{lem:pic0_isAlbanese_all_points}. Together these seven data form the
155	  required witness.
156	\end{proof}
157	
158	\begin{remark}[What the pointed witness settles and what it leaves open]
159	  \label{rem:pointed_witness_scope}
160	  \uses{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint, lem:curve_hypothesis_gap,
161	    def:inst_has_pic_scheme}
162	  \Cref{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint} separates the construction of
163	  the witness from the question of where the rational point comes from, and the two
164	  witnesses below are the two answers to that question:
165	  \cref{def:picardJacobianWitness} takes the point from
166	  \cref{lem:curve_hypothesis_gap} and \cref{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfIsAlgClosed}
167	  from \cref{lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed}. Nothing beyond the choice of
168	  source distinguishes them.
169	
170	  This bears on the open question of \cref{rem:rational_point_scope}
171	  asymmetrically, and the asymmetry is worth recording. A theorem for a curve
172	  \emph{with} a rational point is exactly the statement above, so that formulation
173	  requires no mathematics beyond the obligations already listed there. The étale
174	  formulation is not obtained from it: representing
175	  \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\) replaces \cref{def:inst_has_pic_scheme} rather than
176	  supplying its hypothesis, so it needs a representability theorem for a different
177	  functor. That one formulation is nearer to hand is not an argument that it is the
178	  right claim to make.
179	\end{remark}
180	
181	\begin{theorem}[The Picard identity component is a Jacobian witness]
182	  \label{def:picardJacobianWitness}
183	  \uses{def:JacobianWitness, def:genus, thm:fga_pic_representability,
184	    thm:pic0_isAbelianVariety, thm:pic_zero_dimension_equals_genus,
185	    thm:albanese_universal_property_northstar}
186	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.picardJacobianWitness}
187	  The identity component \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) carries a Jacobian witness for
188	  \(C\).
189	\end{theorem}
190	
191	\begin{proof}
192	  \uses{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint, lem:curve_hypothesis_gap,
193	    rem:pointed_witness_scope}
194	  Apply \cref{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfHasRationalPoint}, whose rational-point
195	  hypothesis is supplied by \cref{lem:curve_hypothesis_gap}. That hypothesis is the
196	  single genuine gap, and it is a gap only over a general base field: over an
197	  algebraically closed field it is \cref{lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed} and the
198	  witness is \cref{def:picardJacobianWitnessOfIsAlgClosed}.
199	\end{proof}
200	
201	\begin{lemma}[A smooth geometrically irreducible curve is geometrically integral]
202	  \label{lem:curve_geometrically_integral}
203	  \leanok
204	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.geometricallyIntegral_of_curve}
205	  Let \(C\) be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over a field \(k\).
206	  Then \(C\) is geometrically integral over \(k\).
207	\end{lemma}
208	
209	\begin{proof}
210	  \leanok
211	  \uses{lem:smooth_geometrically_reduced}
212	  A smooth morphism is geometrically reduced
213	  (\cref{lem:smooth_geometrically_reduced}), and a morphism that is both
214	  geometrically reduced and geometrically irreducible is geometrically integral:
215	  for every field extension \(K/k\) the base change \(C_K\) is then both reduced
216	  and irreducible, hence integral.
217	\end{proof}
218	
219	\begin{lemma}[A smooth morphism is geometrically reduced]
220	  \label{lem:smooth_geometrically_reduced}
221	  \leanok
222	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.SmoothOfRelativeDimension.geometricallyReduced}
223	  A morphism of schemes \(f\colon X\to Y\) that is smooth of some relative
224	  dimension is geometrically reduced: for every field \(K\) and every morphism
225	  \(\Spec K\to Y\), the base change \(X\times_Y\Spec K\) is a reduced scheme.
226	\end{lemma}
227	
228	\begin{proof}
229	  \leanok
230	  \uses{lem:standard_smooth_over_domain_reduced}
231	  Smoothness is stable under base change, so it suffices to show that a scheme
232	  \(X\) smooth over a field \(K\) is reduced. Reducedness is local, and \(X\) is
233	  covered by affine opens \(\Spec S\) with \(S\) standard smooth over \(K\); each
234	  is reduced by \cref{lem:standard_smooth_over_domain_reduced} applied to the
235	  domain \(K\).
236	\end{proof}
237	
238	\begin{lemma}[A standard smooth algebra over a domain is reduced]
239	  \label{lem:standard_smooth_over_domain_reduced}
240	  \leanok
241	  \lean{Algebra.IsStandardSmooth.isReduced_of_isDomain}
242	  Let \(B\) be a domain and \(S\) a standard smooth \(B\)-algebra. Then \(S\) is
243	  reduced.
244	\end{lemma}
245	
246	\begin{proof}
247	  \leanok
248	  By the structure theorem for standard smooth algebras, \(S\) is étale over a
249	  polynomial ring \(P=B[x_1,\dots,x_n]\), which is again a domain. So it suffices
250	  to prove that a flat, formally unramified \(P\)-algebra \(S\) essentially of
251	  finite type over a domain \(P\) is reduced, étale algebras being flat, formally
252	  unramified and essentially of finite type.
253	
254	  Let \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(P)\). The algebra \(F\otimes_P S\) is formally
255	  unramified and essentially of finite type over the field \(F\), hence reduced.
256	  Since \(S\) is flat over \(P\) and \(P\to F\) is injective, the induced map
257	  \(S\cong P\otimes_P S\to F\otimes_P S\) is injective, so \(S\) embeds into a
258	  reduced ring and is therefore reduced.
259	\end{proof}
260	
261	\begin{lemma}[The curve has a \(k\)-rational point]
262	  \label{lem:curve_hypothesis_gap}
263	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.hasRationalPoint_of_curve}
264	  \uses{def:has_rational_point}
265	  A smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve \(C\) over a field \(k\) has a
266	  \(k\)-rational point.
267	\end{lemma}
268	
269	\begin{proof}
270	  This assertion is \emph{false} as stated. A smooth proper geometrically
271	  integral curve need not have a \(k\)-rational point: a conic over \(\mathbb{Q}\)
272	  with no rational point is a genus-\(0\) example, and there are genus-\(2\)
273	  curves over \(\mathbb{Q}\) with no rational point. Over an algebraically closed
274	  field a rational point always exists, since a curve there is a nonempty
275	  Jacobson space whose closed points are rational.
276	
277	  The lemma is therefore stated here only to name the gap between the hypotheses
278	  of the witness and those of the Picard construction, and it is not provable in
279	  this form. Closing it requires either weakening the claim --- carry
280	  \(C(k) \neq \emptyset\) as a hypothesis of the Jacobian itself, which proves
281	  something weaker than intended --- or replacing the input by a representability
282	  statement that needs no section, namely representability of the \'etale
283	  sheafification (\cref{sec:fga_pic_setup}). That choice is open. The algebraically
284	  closed case is not affected by it and is \cref{lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed}.
285	\end{proof}
286	
287	\begin{lemma}[A curve over an algebraically closed field has a rational point]
288	  \label{lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed}
289	  \leanok
290	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.hasRationalPoint_of_curve_of_isAlgClosed}
291	  \uses{def:has_rational_point}
292	  Let \(C\) be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over an algebraically
293	  closed field \(\bar k\). Then \(C\) has a \(\bar k\)-rational point.
294	\end{lemma}
295	
296	\begin{proof}
297	  \leanok
298	  Geometric irreducibility over the one-point base \(\Spec \bar k\) makes the
299	  underlying space of \(C\) irreducible, in particular nonempty, and smoothness makes
300	  \(C \to \Spec \bar k\) locally of finite type, so that space is a Jacobson space.
301	  A nonempty Jacobson space has a closed point \(x\). Over an algebraically closed
302	  field the residue field at a closed point of a scheme locally of finite type is
303	  \(\bar k\) itself, so \(x\) is the image of a section of \(C \to \Spec \bar k\),
304	  which is the required rational point.
305	\end{proof}
306	
307	\begin{remark}[Which leaf is false and which is merely unproved]
308	  \label{rem:rational_point_scope}
309	  \uses{lem:curve_hypothesis_gap, lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed,
310	    def:inst_has_pic_scheme}
311	  \Cref{lem:curve_hypothesis_gap} and \cref{lem:curve_rational_point_algClosed} state the
312	  same conclusion under different hypotheses, and the pair delimits what is open. Over an
313	  arbitrary base field the statement is false, so it admits no proof and the witness built
314	  on it rests on an inconsistent hypothesis --- its consequences are vacuously true. Over
315	  an algebraically closed field the same statement is a theorem. So the open question is
316	  not the existence of a rational point in general, but which of two formulations is

5: \section{Setup and motivation}
6: \label{sec:fga_pic_setup}
7: 
8: Throughout this chapter, fix a base field \(k\) and a smooth proper geometrically
9: integral curve \(C\) over \(k\) (the curve carrying the Jacobian). The relative
10: Picard presheaf \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k} : (\Sch/k)^{op} \to \Set\) of
11: \cref{chap:Picard_LineBundlePullback} has already been packaged as a
12: set-valued functor and refined to its abelian-group-valued
13: \'etale-sheafified version \(\Pic^\sharp_{(C/k)\et}\) in
14: \cref{chap:Picard_RelPicFunctor}. What remains is to produce a scheme
15: representing it: the \emph{Picard scheme} \(\Pic_{C/k}\). The present chapter
16: packages that assembly, together with the abelian-group-scheme refinement.
17: 
18: \medskip
19: 
20: \textbf{Two routes to representability.} The Picard scheme of a curve can be
21: constructed in two ways, and this blueprint records both, because they need
22: different inputs and only one of them is the route under construction here.
23: 
24: The \emph{quotient route} is Grothendieck's, as presented by Kleiman \S 4: the
25: Abel map \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k} \to \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) exhibits the Picard functor
26: as a quotient of a quasi-projective scheme by a smooth proper equivalence
27: relation, and Altman--Kleiman descent
28: (\cref{lem:smooth_proper_quotient}) represents the quotient. Its engine is the
29: Hilbert scheme \(\Hilb_{C/k} = \Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\) of
30: \cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme}, whose open subscheme \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) of
31: relative effective divisors carries the source of the Abel map. This is the route
32: of \cref{thm:fga_pic_representability} and its proof below.
33: 
34: The \emph{Milne--Koll\'ar route} builds \(\Pic^r_{C/k}\) directly, over a
35: separably closed field, from the open loci
36: \[
37:   C^\Sigma = \{\,t : h^0(\mathcal{O}(W - \Sigma)_t) = 1\,\}
38: \]
39: cut out inside a degree-\(r\) divisor scheme by a tuple \(\Sigma\) of rational
40: points, glues them, and descends the result to \(k\) by a finite Galois quotient
41: before assembling the degrees by a coproduct. Its inputs are a rigidified
42: pushforward engine, uniform \(H^1\) vanishing, and Galois descent of rigidified
43: classes --- not a Hilbert or Quot scheme. Its structure, and the parts of it that
44: are established, are the subject of \cref{sec:fga_pic_milne_kollar}.
45: 
46: The decisive difference is the quotient step. Altman--Kleiman descent needs
47: quasi-projectivity of the scheme being quotiented, which is not expressible in
48: the formalisation at present and without which the lemma is false
49: (\cref{rem:smooth_proper_quotient_hypothesis}); the Milne--Koll\'ar route takes
50: only finite Galois quotients under an orbit-in-affine hypothesis, and so avoids
51: that obstruction entirely. The Lean development therefore pursues the
52: Milne--Koll\'ar route. The quotient-route material below is retained as the
53: mathematics it is --- the divisor and Hilbert-scheme substrate it rests on is
54: consumed by both routes --- and is not the path currently being formalised.
55: 
56: \medskip
57: 
58: \textbf{Comparison with the sheafified Picard functor.} Kleiman \S 4 represents
59: the \'etale-sheafified functor \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\). This chapter instead
60: works throughout under the standing hypothesis that \emph{\(C\) has a
61: \(k\)-rational point} (\cref{def:has_rational_point}) and states
62: representability against the \emph{plain} relative Picard functor
63: \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) of \cref{def:rel_pic_sharp}. This is justified by
64: Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5 (\texttt{th:comp}): if \(f : X \to S\) has a section
65: and \(\mathcal O_{S'} = f'_* \mathcal O_{X'}\) holds for all base changes
66: (automatic for our proper geometrically integral curve, by cohomology and
67: base change), then the comparison maps
68: \[
69:   \Pic_{X/S}(T) \longrightarrow \Pic_{(X/S)\et}(T) \longrightarrow
70:   \Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}(T)
71: \]
72: are bijective for every \(T\). Hence under the rational-point hypothesis the
73: plain relative functor \emph{is} the \'etale sheaf, so the rational point
74: allows us to work directly with \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\).
75: 
76: The hypothesis is not a convenience: without a section the plain functor is not
77: even a Zariski sheaf in general, so a representability statement for
78: \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) with no rational point would be false. Two honest
79: formulations are therefore available, and they prove different theorems.
80: 
81: \begin{enumerate}
82:   \item Represent \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) and carry \(C(k) \neq \emptyset\) as a
83:     hypothesis. This is the formulation of
84:     \cref{thm:fga_pic_representability} and of every representability assertion
85:     in this chapter. It is strictly weaker than a statement about all smooth
86:     proper geometrically integral curves, since such a curve need not have a
87:     rational point --- a conic without rational points, or a genus-\(2\) curve
88:     over \(\mathbb{Q}\) with no rational point, satisfies every other
89:     hypothesis.
90:   \item Represent the \'etale sheafification \(\Pic_{(C/k)\et}\) and drop the
91:     rational point. This is Kleiman's own formulation, and needs no section
92:     precisely because sheafifying supplies \'etale-locally what the section
93:     would have supplied globally. It requires developing the Picard functor on
94:     the \'etale site.
95: \end{enumerate}
96: 
97: Which formulation the project should target is a decision about what theorem is
98: being claimed, not a limitation of the platform. The two are recorded here
99: side by side; the chapter as written realises the first.
100: 
101: Every representability assertion of this chapter accordingly carries the
102: rational-point hypothesis. A pointed curve \((C,P)\), as in
103: \cref{chap:AbelJacobi}, supplies such a section.
104: 
105: % SOURCE: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 4 (FGA Explained Ch.~9 \S 9.4);
106: % arXiv:math/0504020, p.~26. Read from
107: % references/kleiman-picard-src/kleiman-picard.tex.

109: \section{Line bundles and the Quot / Hilbert scheme}
110: \label{sec:fga_pic_line_bundle_quot}
111: 
112: The bridge from line bundles on \(C \times_k T\) to the Quot scheme is the
113: Abel map: a relative effective divisor \(D \subset C \times_k T\) over \(T\)
114: (a \(T\)-flat closed subscheme whose ideal is invertible) determines a closed
115: subscheme of \(C \times_k T\) flat over \(T\), hence a \(T\)-point of the Hilbert
116: functor \(\Hilb_{C/k}(T)\), which is the special case \(\Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\)
117: of the Quot functor of \cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme}; and it determines an
118: invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_{C \times_k T}(D)\) on the relative curve,
119: representing a class in \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}(T)\).
120: 
121: \begin{definition}[Abel-map witness]\leanok
122:   \label{def:abel_map_witness}
123:   \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.PicScheme.abelMapWitness}
124:   \uses{def:div_functor_carrier, def:pic_sharp_carrier}
125:   Let \(C/k\) be a smooth proper curve. Define a
126:   natural transformation
127:   \[
128:     A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{C/k} \colon \mathrm{Div}_{C/k}
129:       \longrightarrow \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}
130:   \]
131:   as the composite
132:   \(
133:     \mathrm{abelKernelNatTrans}(C)
134:     \mathbin{;} \mathrm{picNeg}(C)
135:   \).
136: \end{definition}
137: 
138: \begin{proof}\leanok
139:   The first transformation sends the class represented by
140:   \(\langle \mathcal F,q\rangle\) to \([\ker q]\). It is well defined because
141:   equivalent divisor families induce isomorphic kernels. It is natural under
142:   arbitrary base change because the kernel--pullback comparison is an
143:   isomorphism for an epimorphic quotient with finitely presented, base-flat
144:   target and invertible kernel. The second transformation is pointwise
145:   inversion in the group-valued presheaf \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\). Their composite
146:   is therefore natural and sends
147:   \(\langle \mathcal F,q\rangle\) to \(-[\ker q]\).
148: \end{proof}
149: 
150: \begin{lemma}[Line bundle / Quot correspondence via the Abel map]\leanok
151:   \label{lem:line_bundle_quot_correspondence}
152:   \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.PicScheme.abelMap_app_mk}
153:   \uses{def:abel_map_witness, def:inst_has_abel_map, def:has_abel_map,
154:     def:div_functor_carrier, def:pic_sharp_carrier}
155:   % SOURCE: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 3, Def.~dfn:Abel (the Abel
156:   % map), and Thm.~th:repDiv (representability of relative effective
157:   % divisors by an open subscheme of \(\IHilb_{X/S}\)); arXiv:math/0504020,
158:   % pp.~25, 23 (read from
159:   % references/kleiman-picard-src/kleiman-picard.tex, L1837-L1841 + L2135-L2145).
160:   % Source identifiers: \begin{thm}\label{th:repDiv}\end{thm}
161:   % and \begin{dfn}\label{dfn:Abel}\end{dfn}.
162:   \textit{Source: [Kleiman], ``The Picard scheme'', \S 3,
163:   Thm.~3.7 + Def.~4.6 (cf.\ [Nitsure], ``Construction of Hilbert
164:   and Quot Schemes'', \S 1, where \(\Hilb_{X/S} = \Quot_{\mathcal{O}_X/X/S}\)).}
165:   Let \(C/k\) be a smooth proper geometrically integral curve. There is a
166:   natural transformation of presheaves on \((\Sch/k)^{op}\)
167:   \[
168:     A_{C/k} = \mathrm{abelMap} \;\colon\; \mathrm{Div}_{C/k}
169:       \;\longrightarrow\; \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}
170:   \]
171:   (\(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) the relative-divisor functor of
172:   \cref{def:div_functor_carrier}, \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) the relative
173:   Picard functor of \cref{def:pic_sharp_carrier}), with the following
174:   \emph{defining property}: at a \(T\)-point represented by a family
175:   \(\langle \mathcal F, q\rangle\) (\cref{def:div_family}: a finitely
176:   presented, \(T\)-flat quotient
177:   \(q \colon \mathcal O_{C\times_kT}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal F\)
178:   whose kernel is an invertible ideal sheaf cutting out a relative effective
179:   divisor \(D\subseteq C\times_kT\)),
180:   \[
181:     A_{C/k}(T)\bigl(\langle \mathcal F, q\rangle\bigr)
182:       \;=\; -[\ker q] \;=\; [(\ker q)^{-1}]
183:       \;=\; \bigl[\mathcal{O}_{C \times_k T}(D)\bigr]
184:       \;\in\; \Pic^\sharp_{C/k}(T),
185:   \]
186:   the class of the associated invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_{C \times_k
187:   T}(D)\), i.e.\ the additive inverse of the class of the ideal sheaf
188:   \(\ker q\) (Kleiman \S 3, Def.~dfn:Abel). This transformation is the
189:   required witness for \(\mathrm{HasAbelMap}(C)\)
190:   (\cref{def:has_abel_map}).
191: \end{lemma}
192: 
193: \begin{proof}
194:   The instance of \cref{def:inst_has_abel_map} identifies
195:   \(A_{C/k}\) with the witness of \cref{def:abel_map_witness}. Evaluating its
196:   two factors at \(\langle \mathcal F,q\rangle\) first gives the kernel class
197:   \([\ker q]\) and then its inverse. Since the kernel is the ideal sheaf of
198:   \(D\), its inverse is \(\mathcal O_{C\times_kT}(D)\), which gives the stated
199:   formula.
200: \end{proof}

202: \begin{remark}
203: [Representability of \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\)]
204:   \label{rem:div_functor_representability}
205:   Kleiman~\S 3, Thm.~th:repDiv, shows that \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) is
206:   representable by an open subscheme \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k} \subseteq
207:   \Hilb_{C/k}\) of the Hilbert scheme (\(\Hilb_{C/k} =
208:   \Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\), \cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme}): letting
209:   \(W \subseteq C \times_k \Hilb_{C/k}\) be the universal closed
210:   subscheme and \(q \colon W \to \Hilb_{C/k}\) the projection, the locus
211:   \(V \subseteq W\) where \(W\) is locally an effective Cartier divisor
212:   is open, so \(Z := q(W \setminus V)\) is closed (\(q\) proper) and
213:   \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k} := \Hilb_{C/k} \setminus Z\) is the open
214:   subscheme representing relative effective divisors. This is
215:   the relative-divisor functor appearing in
216:   \cref{def:div_functor_carrier}.
217: \end{remark}
